conventions.outcomes: Overall outcome is one of outcome_vocabulary (04 §11.2). Mapping from 08 §7: eligible -> eligible; ineligible -> not_eligible | already_completed | temporarily_excluded; indeterminate -> insufficient_evidence | requires_clinical_review; engine error -> evaluation_error. Criterion-level outcomes (08 §7.1): passed | failed | unknown | not_applicable | error.
conventions.evaluation_date: Always explicit (08 §9.2). resident.age = completed years at evaluation_date from a verified date of birth; unknown if the date of birth is missing or its precision leaves the age on both sides of a threshold. Regression cases use 2026-11-08.
conventions.resident_fields: resident.age; resident.sex_assigned_at_birth (female|male|unknown). The engine populates sex_assigned_at_birth from residents.sex ONLY for Synthea-generated data (assumption A-02, see population_applicability.synthea_mapping); for any non-synthetic source the us-core-birthsex value must be used and a missing value is 'unknown'.
conventions.three_valued_logic: Expressions evaluate to true | false | unknown with Kleene logic: AND(false,unknown)=false, AND(true,unknown)=unknown, OR(true,unknown)=true, OR(false,unknown)=unknown, NOT(unknown)=unknown. A leaf over a missing/unknown value is unknown.
conventions.rule_result_to_outcome: Each rule has criterion_semantics (expression result -> criterion outcome) AND outcome_by_expression_result (expression result -> overall-outcome contribution; null = none). decision_policy ranks contributions; reason_code / reason_code_when_unknown name the cause; explanation_templates hold the approved explanation text (never LLM-written).
conventions.expression_leaf_format: {field, operator, value}; operators exactly those of 08 §6.3. Extensions to confirm with the engine owner: (1) EXISTS with field 'evidence.selector' and value = selector name; (2) aggregate fields evidence.<selector>.{latest_event_date, distinct_subjects, min_age_at_onset, early_start_age, shared_subjects.<other selector>}; (3) DATE_WITHIN value {'years': N, optional 'range_years': [min,max], 'basis': 'max'} meaning date in (evaluation_date - N years, evaluation_date]; (4) value may be {'field': ...}.
conventions.selector_semantics: A selector (selector_library) picks facts by category, fact_type, optional codes, subject_type, relationship, assertion_status, temporal_status. Validation: 'accepted' facts are definite; pending/schema_valid/source_verified/requires_review facts are UNRESOLVED candidates; rejected/failed facts are ignored (08 §10.1, §16.4 test 6; policy.py: only accepted facts may feed rules). Structured FHIR evidence is assumed accepted by ingestion. A fact whose relationship is in unresolved_relationship_in is an unresolved candidate. EXISTS = true if >=1 definite fact and no conflict; unknown if no definite fact but an unresolved candidate exists, or if definite positive and negative facts about the same subject conflict; false otherwise. Facts that arrived from clinical notes (AI-extracted) and facts from structured records are treated identically once accepted.
conventions.aggregate_semantics: Subject key = subject_person_id, else relationship. distinct_subjects and shared_subjects are evaluated with interval semantics [definite, definite + unresolved-only subjects]. min_age_at_onset is the minimum over subjects with exactly ONE consistent age_at_onset; a subject with a missing age, two different ages across documents, or only unresolved facts makes the minimum an interval (-infinity, known_min]: comparisons that the interval cannot decide are unknown; with no subjects at all the minimum is +infinity. early_start_age = min(40, min_age_at_onset - 10) and is unknown if any subject is unresolved. Date comparisons use the full range of a partial date; if the range straddles the window edge the result is unknown; an undated definite fact makes the result unknown unless another fact already satisfies the window.
conventions.interval_convention: Intervals are stored as single values or ranges (min_years, max_years). Deterministic due-date convention: due_date = last_event_date + max_years (calendar years), 'up to date' through the due date inclusive; outreach is never created before it. min_years is metadata for reviewers/alternative conventions. Stool DNA-FIT: range 1-3 years stored, max (3) used.
conventions.documented_record_semantics: D-01. Three deliberate places where absence of evidence changes an outcome: (1) no exclusion fact -> the exclusion does not apply; (2) no completion fact -> 'no documented completion'; (3) no trigger fact -> a history-conditional pathway is 'not applicable'. The explanation must say 'no documented X', never 'X did not occur', and engagement must ask the resident/clinician to confirm. All other missing evidence yields unknown -> insufficient_evidence. Unsourced clinical-logic exclusions (total colectomy, bilateral mastectomy) route to requires_clinical_review instead of excluding.
conventions.fact_type_vocabulary: fact_type values are PROPOSED canonical snake_case names; the evidence workstream must emit or normalize to them. Category and relationship vocabularies follow backend/anticipa/evidence/schemas.py.
conventions.code_verification: synthea_module+ontoserver: the code appears in a Synthea module (master @ bd8a52b, 2026-10-21) AND exists in the SNOMED CT/LOINC release served by the public CSIRO Ontoserver on 2026-11-08. ontoserver_only: exists in terminology but Synthea does not emit it. unverified: not checked.

owner_decisions.summary: Documented-record semantics (see conventions) vs strict 'indeterminate for any absence'; 5-year record-coverage prerequisite (assumption A-01).

USPSTF 'average risk' excludes only KNOWN GENETIC disorders; residents with a documented first-degree relative (or a relative of unspecified degree) are deferred to the USMSTF family-history guideline; second-degree-only relatives stay in the average-risk rule (owner-directed).
sDNA-FIT range 1-3 years stored, due date = last test + 3 years. Flexible sigmoidoscopy USPSTF 5y vs USMSTF 5-10y (5 used). 'Sigmoidoscopy q10y + annual FIT' not modelled.
USPSTF 2021, ACS 2018 and USMSTF 2022 say 45; USMSTF 2017 said 50 (45 for African Americans). 45 used.
USPSTF 2024: biennial from 40. ACS: annual 45-54 (option at 40-44), then biennial or annual. USPSTF used.
USPSTF 2018 FINAL used. The 2024 USPSTF document is a DRAFT (not used): primary HPV q5y from 30, patient-collected samples. ACS 2020 starts at 25.
Colonoscopy/mammography/HPV with unspecified indication count as completion; symptomatic/diagnostic mammography does not.

Trigger has no degree-of-relationship limit (source silent). Tool modelled: FHS-7 exactly as published (one positive item). Stage 2 also accepts a clinician-documented positive result of any USPSTF-listed tool. No reassessment interval in the source.
Total colectomy and bilateral mastectomy are not in the cited sources; they route to requires_clinical_review (v1 excluded automatically).
No age range found in the USPSTF text read; adults (18+) assumed.
Breast/BRCA: source population is stated by sex assigned at birth (quoted). Cervical: proxy for 'having a cervix'. Synthea has a single M/F attribute.
Synthea emits almost no screening history or family history for eligible people; the Anticipa generator must plant them (README).
All sources are US guidelines; applicability to the India/Gulf demo setting is not assessed.

excerpts.text: The USPSTF recommends screening for colorectal cancer in all adults aged 50 to 75 years.
The USPSTF recommends screening for colorectal cancer in adults aged 45 to 49 years.
The USPSTF recommends that clinicians selectively offer screening for colorectal cancer in adults aged 76 to 85 years.

This recommendation applies to asymptomatic adults 45 years or older who are at average risk of colorectal cancer (ie, no prior diagnosis of colorectal cancer, adenomatous polyps, or inflammatory bowel disease; no personal diagnosis or family history of known genetic disorders that predispose them to a high lifetime risk of colorectal cancer [such as Lynch syndrome or familial adenomatous polyposis]).
Colonoscopy screening every 10 years
High-sensitivity gFOBT or FIT every year
sDNA-FIT every 1 to 3 years
CT colonography every 5 years
Flexible sigmoidoscopy every 5 years
Flexible sigmoidoscopy every 10 years + FIT every year
When stool-based tests reveal abnormal results, follow-up with colonoscopy is needed for further evaluation.

In adults 86 years or older, evidence on benefits and harms of colorectal cancer screening is lacking, and competing causes of mortality likely preclude any survival benefit that would outweigh the harms of screening.
persons with a family history of colorectal cancer (even in the absence of any known inherited syndrome such as Lynch syndrome or familial adenomatous polyposis)

excerpts.text: Persons with a family history of CRC or a documented advanced adenoma in a first-degree relative age <60 years or 2 first-degree relatives with these findings at any age are recommended to undergo screening by colonoscopy every 5 years, beginning 10 years before the age at diagnosis of the youngest affected relative or age 40, whichever is earlier.
Persons with a single first-degree relative diagnosed at ≥60 years with CRC or an advanced adenoma can be offered average-risk screening options beginning at age 40 years.
Screening should begin at age 50 years in average-risk persons, except in African Americans in whom limited evidence supports screening at 45 years.
The second-tier tests include CT colonography every 5 years, the FIT-fecal DNA test every 3 years, and flexible sigmoidoscopy every 5 to 10 years.

Discontinuation of screening should be considered when persons up to date with screening, who have prior negative screening (particularly colonoscopy), reach age 75 or have <10 years of life expectancy.

excerpts.text: Persons with a family history of CRC or a documented advanced adenoma in a first-degree relative age <60 years or 2 first-degree relatives with these findings at any age are recommended to undergo screening by colonoscopy every 5 years, beginning 10 years before the age at diagnosis of the youngest affected relative or age 40, whichever is earlier.
Persons with a single first-degree relative diagnosed at ≥60 years with CRC or an advanced adenoma can be offered average-risk screening options beginning at age 40 years.
Screening should begin at age 50 years in average-risk persons, except in African Americans in whom limited evidence supports screening at 45 years.
The second-tier tests include CT colonography every 5 years, the FIT-fecal DNA test every 3 years, and flexible sigmoidoscopy every 5 to 10 years.

Discontinuation of screening should be considered when persons up to date with screening, who have prior negative screening (particularly colonoscopy), reach age 75 or have <10 years of life expectancy.

excerpts.text: The USPSTF recommends screening for colorectal cancer in all adults aged 50 to 75 years.
The USPSTF recommends screening for colorectal cancer in adults aged 45 to 49 years.
The USPSTF recommends that clinicians selectively offer screening for colorectal cancer in adults aged 76 to 85 years.

This recommendation applies to asymptomatic adults 45 years or older who are at average risk of colorectal cancer (ie, no prior diagnosis of colorectal cancer, adenomatous polyps, or inflammatory bowel disease; no personal diagnosis or family history of known genetic disorders that predispose them to a high lifetime risk of colorectal cancer [such as Lynch syndrome or familial adenomatous polyposis]).
Colonoscopy screening every 10 years
High-sensitivity gFOBT or FIT every year
sDNA-FIT every 1 to 3 years
CT colonography every 5 years
Flexible sigmoidoscopy every 5 years
Flexible sigmoidoscopy every 10 years + FIT every year
When stool-based tests reveal abnormal results, follow-up with colonoscopy is needed for further evaluation.

In adults 86 years or older, evidence on benefits and harms of colorectal cancer screening is lacking, and competing causes of mortality likely preclude any survival benefit that would outweigh the harms of screening.

sources.title: Breast Cancer: Screening — Final Recommendation Statement

excerpts.text: The USPSTF recommends biennial screening mammography for women aged 40 to 74 years.
The USPSTF concludes that the current evidence is insufficient to assess the balance of benefits and harms of screening mammography in women 75 years or older.

They also apply to women who have factors associated with an increased risk of breast cancer, such as a family history of breast cancer (ie, a first-degree relative with breast cancer) or having dense breasts.

These recommendations do not apply to persons who have a genetic marker or syndrome associated with a high risk of breast cancer (eg, BRCA1 or BRCA2 genetic variation), a history of high-dose radiation therapy to the chest at a young age, or previous breast cancer or a high-risk breast lesion on previous biopsies.
Screen women aged 40 to 74 with a mammogram every 2 years.
The American Cancer Society recommends that women with an average risk of breast cancer should undergo regular screening mammography starting at age 45 years.
These recommendations apply to cisgender women and all other persons assigned female at birth (including transgender men and nonbinary persons) 40 years or older at average risk of breast cancer.

excerpts.text: The USPSTF recommends that primary care clinicians assess women with a personal or family history of breast, ovarian, tubal, or peritoneal cancer or who have an ancestry associated with breast cancer susceptibility 1 and 2 (BRCA1/2) gene mutations with an appropriate brief familial risk assessment tool.
Women with a positive result on the risk assessment tool should receive genetic counseling and, if indicated after counseling, genetic testing.

The USPSTF recommends against routine risk assessment, genetic counseling, or genetic testing for women whose personal or family history or ancestry is not associated with potentially harmful BRCA1/2 gene mutations.
This recommendation applies to women who are asymptomatic for BRCA-related cancer and have unknown BRCA mutation status.

It includes women who have never been diagnosed with BRCA-related cancer, as well as those with a previous breast, ovarian, tubal, or peritoneal cancer diagnosis who have completed treatment and are considered cancer free but have not been previously tested.

These include breast cancer diagnosis before age 50 years, bilateral breast cancer, presence of both breast and ovarian cancer in one individual, male family members with breast cancer, multiple cases of breast cancer in the family, 1 or more family members with 2 primary types of BRCA-related cancer (such as ovarian cancer), and Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry.
The USPSTF recognizes that each risk assessment tool has advantages and limitations and found insufficient evidence to recommend one over another.

Tools evaluated by the USPSTF include the Ontario Family History Assessment Tool, Manchester Scoring System, Referral Screening Tool, Pedigree Assessment Tool, 7-Question Family History Screening Tool, International Breast Cancer Intervention Study instrument (Tyrer-Cuzick), and brief versions of BRCAPRO.

The updated recommendation expands the population eligible for screening to include women with a previous breast, ovarian, tubal, or peritoneal cancer diagnosis who have completed treatment and are considered cancer free and more explicitly includes ancestry associated with BRCA1/2 mutations (ie, founder mutations) as a risk factor.
Did any of your first-degree relatives have breast or ovarian cancer?
Did any of your relatives have bilateral breast cancer?
Did any man in your family have breast cancer?
Did any woman in your family have breast and ovarian cancer?
Did any woman in your family have breast cancer before age 50 y?
Do you have 2 or more relatives with breast and/or ovarian cancer?
Do you have 2 or more relatives with breast and/or bowel cancer?
One positive response initiates referral.
Each of these tools has been validated and accurately estimate the likelihood of carrying a harmful BRCA1/2 mutation.
Persons should consider their sex at birth to determine which recommendation best applies to them.

excerpts.text: The USPSTF recommends that primary care clinicians assess women with a personal or family history of breast, ovarian, tubal, or peritoneal cancer or who have an ancestry associated with breast cancer susceptibility 1 and 2 (BRCA1/2) gene mutations with an appropriate brief familial risk assessment tool.
Women with a positive result on the risk assessment tool should receive genetic counseling and, if indicated after counseling, genetic testing.

The USPSTF recommends against routine risk assessment, genetic counseling, or genetic testing for women whose personal or family history or ancestry is not associated with potentially harmful BRCA1/2 gene mutations.
This recommendation applies to women who are asymptomatic for BRCA-related cancer and have unknown BRCA mutation status.

It includes women who have never been diagnosed with BRCA-related cancer, as well as those with a previous breast, ovarian, tubal, or peritoneal cancer diagnosis who have completed treatment and are considered cancer free but have not been previously tested.

These include breast cancer diagnosis before age 50 years, bilateral breast cancer, presence of both breast and ovarian cancer in one individual, male family members with breast cancer, multiple cases of breast cancer in the family, 1 or more family members with 2 primary types of BRCA-related cancer (such as ovarian cancer), and Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry.
The USPSTF recognizes that each risk assessment tool has advantages and limitations and found insufficient evidence to recommend one over another.

Tools evaluated by the USPSTF include the Ontario Family History Assessment Tool, Manchester Scoring System, Referral Screening Tool, Pedigree Assessment Tool, 7-Question Family History Screening Tool, International Breast Cancer Intervention Study instrument (Tyrer-Cuzick), and brief versions of BRCAPRO.

The updated recommendation expands the population eligible for screening to include women with a previous breast, ovarian, tubal, or peritoneal cancer diagnosis who have completed treatment and are considered cancer free and more explicitly includes ancestry associated with BRCA1/2 mutations (ie, founder mutations) as a risk factor.
Did any of your first-degree relatives have breast or ovarian cancer?
Did any of your relatives have bilateral breast cancer?
Did any man in your family have breast cancer?
Did any woman in your family have breast and ovarian cancer?
Did any woman in your family have breast cancer before age 50 y?
Do you have 2 or more relatives with breast and/or ovarian cancer?
Do you have 2 or more relatives with breast and/or bowel cancer?
One positive response initiates referral.
Each of these tools has been validated and accurately estimate the likelihood of carrying a harmful BRCA1/2 mutation.
Persons should consider their sex at birth to determine which recommendation best applies to them.

excerpts.text: The USPSTF recommends screening for cervical cancer every 3 years with cervical cytology alone in women aged 21 to 29 years.

For women aged 30 to 65 years, the USPSTF recommends screening every 3 years with cervical cytology alone, every 5 years with high-risk human papillomavirus (hrHPV) testing alone, or every 5 years with hrHPV testing in combination with cytology (cotesting).
The USPSTF recommends against screening for cervical cancer in women younger than 21 years.

The USPSTF recommends against screening for cervical cancer in women who have had a hysterectomy with removal of the cervix and do not have a history of a high-grade precancerous lesion (ie, cervical intraepithelial neoplasia [CIN] grade 2 or 3) or cervical cancer.
The USPSTF recommends against screening for cervical cancer in women older than 65 years who have had adequate prior screening and are not otherwise at high risk for cervical cancer.

This recommendation statement applies to all asymptomatic individuals with a cervix, regardless of their sexual history. This recommendation statement does not apply to women who have been diagnosed with a high-grade precancerous cervical lesion or cervical cancer, women with in utero exposure to diethylstilbestrol, or women who have a compromised immune system (eg, women living with HIV).
As part of the clinical evaluation, clinicians should confirm through review of surgical records or direct examination that the cervix was removed.

Joint guidelines from the American Cancer Society, American Society for Colposcopy and Cervical Pathology, and American Society for Clinical Pathology (ACS/ASCCP/ASCP) define adequate prior screening as 3 consecutive negative cytology results or 2 consecutive negative cotesting results within 10 years before stopping screening, with the most recent test occurring within 5 years.

The guidelines further state that routine screening should continue for at least 20 years after spontaneous regression or appropriate management of a precancerous lesion, even if this extends screening past age 65 years.

Certain considerations may also support screening in women older than 65 years who are otherwise at high risk (ie, women with a history of high-grade precancerous lesions or cervical cancer, in utero exposure to diethylstilbestrol, or a compromised immune system).

Women who have had a hysterectomy with removal of the cervix and do not have a history of a high-grade precancerous lesion or cervical cancer are not at risk for cervical cancer and should not be screened.
